lead.headline: Millions of Grown-Ups Are Already Voting
lead.deck: The midterm elections are on 3 November, but many people have voted early.
body: On 3 November, grown-ups in the United States will vote in the midterm elections. They choose people for Congress. Congress is the group that makes the country's laws. Midterms come halfway through a president's four years in office.

Many people do not wait for the last day. They vote early, by mail or in person. A group at the University of Florida counts early votes. It found more than 16 million people in 41 states and Washington, D.C. had already voted. About 10 million voted by mail. About 6 million voted in person.

Some places have seen big jumps. The Associated Press, a news agency, found huge jumps in Kansas and Texas. In Maine, North Carolina and Ohio there were at least 30% more early votes than four years ago.

lead.why: Voting is how people choose who makes the laws. Children cannot vote yet, but they can learn how it works.

science.headline: A Robot Rover Sets a Driving Record on Mars
science.deck: Perseverance has now driven farther than any rover before it.
body: A rover is a robot car that explores another world. NASA's rover Perseverance is on Mars. On 11 October, it passed a driving record. It has driven 28.10 miles. An older rover named Opportunity drove 28.06 miles.

Perseverance took about five and a half years. Opportunity took nearly 15 years. The new rover is faster because it can steer itself. It used its own driving system for more than 90% of the trip. Opportunity used its own system for about 5% of its trip.

NASA first planned for the rover to drive no more than 12.4 miles. The mission has been extended to about the end of 2028. Next, Perseverance is heading for a huge block of ancient rock called Rainbow Falls. It is about as wide as a football field is long.

science.why: A rover that picks safe paths by itself can explore much more ground.

world.headline: More Giant Tortoises Than People Live on Aldabra
world.deck: A survey counted about 183,000 of them on a remote island ring.
body: Seychelles is a country of islands in the Indian Ocean. Aldabra is part of it. It is an atoll, a ring of coral islands around a lagoon. Scientists now think about 183,000 giant tortoises live there.

That is more than the number of people in Seychelles, which is about 123,000. The scientists used five years of counts, from 2018 to 2022. They also used math to guess how many tortoises hide in thick bushes. So the number is an estimate, which means a careful guess.

The tortoises nearly vanished. In the 1800s people took far too many, and fewer than 1,000 were left. Aldabra became a nature reserve in 1981. In 2012, people removed invasive goats from the island. Today the population looks steady.

illustration.title: ISLAND OF TORTOISES
illustration.subtitle: Aldabra, Seychelles
illustration.caption: A ring of coral islands in the Indian Ocean.

world.connect: Protecting a place can bring animals back. Aldabra became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1982.

challenge.title: BE A ROVER DRIVER
body: Build a small obstacle course with cushions and shoes. One person is the rover and wears a blindfold or closes their eyes. The other is Mission Control and may only say three commands: forward, left, right. Can the rover reach the end without a bump?
Now try a rover that steers itself. Walk slowly and look for a safe path alone. Which way was easier, and why? Then count how many steps it took. Perseverance's whole trip so far is 28.10 miles.

sources.title: NASA's Perseverance Sets Off-World Record for Total Distance Driven

did_you_know.text: The first Mars rover, Sojourner, drove only about 330 feet in 1997. That is about as long as a football field.

explainer.title: HOW A ROVER DRIVES ITSELF
body: Mars is far away. A radio message from Earth takes many minutes to get there. So engineers cannot steer a rover like a toy car.

Instead, the rover looks at the ground around it and picks a safe path. Perseverance looks at 600,000 measurement points each time. Sojourner, the first Mars rover, looked at 20. Looking at more points helps a rover avoid rocks.
